The TCS Paper Archive

Sixty-six years of theoretical computer science in one place: complete bibliographic records for — papers from five top conferences, and a daily briefing on what went up on arXiv this morning. Conference metadata comes from DBLP, preprints from arXiv; topic labels are keyword rules over titles.

01 / Digest

The shape of the day

Written by a model from the day's titles and topic counts. Use it to find a direction, not as a finding — every claim belongs to the paper it came from.

02 / Picked

Worth reading first

The order comes from keyword rules — whether the authors publish repeatedly at FOCS/STOC/SODA/ITCS/EC, whether the abstract claims an open problem resolved, a first, or an optimal bound, and whether the primary category is core TCS. Every paper's score breaks down on the card, so nothing here is a black box. This ranks what to open first, not paper quality.

03 / Everything

Every paper from the day

Papers outside the picks carry only their rule-based topic labels — no model write-up. Abstracts expand in place.

01 / Scale

Sixty-six years of output

Papers accepted per year at each conference. SODA started in 1990 and ITCS joined in 2010; together with each venue growing on its own, annual output climbed from a few dozen papers in the 1960s to more than eight hundred today.

    02 / Composition

    What the papers are about

    Papers matched per topic, across 24 topics. One paper can belong to several topics at once (— on average), so the parts add up to more than the whole. — of all papers match at least one topic.

    03 / Evolution

    How topics shift across the decades

    Read along a row: each cell's shade is that topic's share of the five-year period relative to the topic's own historical peak, so one row traces a single field's rise and fall. For absolute scale across topics see the previous section — shades are not comparable between rows. Early periods have small samples, so they swing more.

    04 / Specialization

    Each conference's fingerprint

    Measured as specialization: the topic's share within a conference ÷ its share across all papers. A value of 2.0 means the conference publishes that topic at twice the overall rate. Only topics with at least 20 papers at that conference are shown.

    05 / Vocabulary

    Terms heating up and cooling down

    Comparing 2014–2026 against 1995–2013: the ratio between how often a term appears per thousand paper titles. This counts words, it does not read them — the same idea under a new name is counted as two different terms.

    Data sources

    All conference metadata was fetched from DBLP's official search API, covering every proceedings of FOCS, STOC, SODA, ITCS (conf/innovations in DBLP) and EC (conf/sigecom), crawled in August 2026. The daily tab comes from arXiv's Atom API instead, taking everything first submitted that day to cs.CC, cs.DS, cs.DM, cs.GT and cs.CG.

    DBLP carries no abstracts, so those come from OpenAlex, matched by DOI where one exists and otherwise by exact title and year. About — of papers have one; the rest show no abstract toggle at all. Abstracts load on demand, so the browser fetches them only for papers you open.

    Where the topic labels come from

    Hand-written regular expressions matched against paper titles; one paper can match several topics. This is a rough heuristic classification, not a semantic model: papers whose titles omit the keywords are missed, and ambiguous words produce false matches. About a quarter of all papers fall under no topic at all, and that share is much higher in the early decades. Read the trends as orders of magnitude, not as precise measurements.

    How the daily tab is built

    Three layers, each of which degrades on its own. arXiv's API supplies the day's new submissions; keyword rules assign topics and a score; and only the top fifteen go to a model, which writes the result, method and significance lines from the abstract alone — it has not read the paper.

    So it can misread, restate an author's claim as established fact, or garble a formula, and the star rating is its opinion, not peer review. These are preprints: nothing here has been refereed. Treat the tab as a filter and open what interests you on arXiv.

    Known caveats

    Paper counts follow DBLP entries, with the proceedings' own editorship and its front-matter and table-of-contents entries removed — though some one-page abstracts remain, most noticeably at EC. Authors are deduplicated by DBLP author ID, so distinct people who share a name are not wrongly merged.
